lenovo-2b-convertible-bonds-2026.headline: Lenovo raises $2 billion from seven-year convertible bond offering
lenovo-2b-convertible-bonds-2026.body_md:
Lenovo Group raised $2 billion through a sale of seven-year zero-coupon convertible bonds this week, the Beijing-based computer and AI server maker's second capital raise of identical size in as many years — and a sign that the company has found a reliable valve in the convertible debt market even as its equity tells a different story.

The bonds, due 2033 and marketed to investors at a conversion premium of 40 to 50 percent above Lenovo's Wednesday close, priced at the tight end: 47.5 percent above the prior closing price, implying a conversion price of HK$36.70 per share. They carry no coupon — meaning Lenovo pays nothing in interest over the seven-year term — and include an investor put option after four years. The bonds are intended to list in Vienna; any shares issued on conversion would list in Hong Kong. JPMorgan, HSBC, BNP Paribas, and DBS Group arranged the deal, which drew orders from more than 160 investors, with allocations heavily weighted toward the top ten.

## Retiring the old debt first

The use of proceeds sharpens the picture. A portion of the new $2 billion will go toward repurchasing up to $675 million of Lenovo's outstanding 2029 convertible bonds — debt the company originally issued at a 2.50 percent coupon. Those bonds are being bought back at 293.2 percent of par, a premium that reflects how deeply in the money they have become: Lenovo's Hong Kong-listed shares have surged roughly 165 percent this year, hitting a 26-year high after full-year revenue rose 20 percent to $83.1 billion and adjusted net profit climbed 42 percent to $2 billion. The company has already secured agreements from holders of about $225 million in principal; approximately $450 million remains outstanding.

Rather than let those bonds convert — which would flood the market with new shares — Lenovo is paying cash to retire them, funded by what amounts to free money: a zero-coupon instrument that costs nothing until 2033. The remainder of the proceeds will go toward on-market share repurchases, subject to shareholder approval at the upcoming annual meeting, a precaution designed to let the company buy back stock without triggering a mandatory general offer under Hong Kong takeover rules.

The prior $2 billion raise, completed in January 2025, went to Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. That deal was structured as a three-year zero-coupon convertible and came packaged with a commitment to build a regional headquarters and manufacturing facility in Riyadh. The current transaction has no such bilateral arrangement — it was placed into the broader institutional market and met with multiple times oversubscription.

Lenovo enters this financing with a $21 billion AI server order pipeline and a stated ambition to reach $100 billion in annual revenue within two years. Investors who received allocations are now effectively betting that the stock will be worth at least 47.5 percent more than today's close by 2033 — a threshold that looks less exotic given the pace of the past twelve months.

The next marker to watch is the annual general meeting, where shareholders will be asked to authorize the buyback mandate. How much of the 2029 bond stock Lenovo ultimately retires — and at what total cost — will be disclosed in the next results announcement.

trump-intel-semiconductor-tariffs.headline: Trump pledges Intel support and tariff shield for domestic chip manufacturing
trump-intel-semiconductor-tariffs.body_md:
On Thursday, President Trump posted on Truth Social that Apple has agreed to work with Intel to design and manufacture chips in the United States — an announcement wrapped in the by-now-familiar charge that Taiwan and others "stole our Semiconductor Factories" while past administrations looked away. "The Technology the World relies on was invented in America," the post read. "We all remember 'Intel Inside.'" Tariffs, Trump said, were the mechanism to fix it.

No tariff rate, no timeline, and no support mechanism for Intel were specified.

## What the policy record actually shows

The tariff architecture is real, if incomplete. In January, the administration issued a Section 232 proclamation putting a 25% levy on specified advanced chips — Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X among them — while carving out imports destined for domestic manufacturing buildout. The exemption was deliberate: the policy is meant to pressure foreign foundries to build on US soil, not to penalise the TSMC fab expansions in Arizona that the same administration championed.

A broader 100% tariff on foreign-made chips has been floated since August 2025. It remains unscheduled. Commerce is running a Section 232 investigation into the broader semiconductor trade picture; a formal finding and accompanying rate schedule have not been published.

On the Intel side, the government already holds roughly a 10% equity stake in the company and has committed approximately $10 billion to domestic factory development. Intel has entered risk production on its 18A process node — the technology it is counting on to regain parity with TSMC and Samsung, and the foundation any Apple manufacturing deal would require.

The Apple-Intel partnership itself is not new news. The Wall Street Journal reported a preliminary deal in May, following more than a year of discussions. What Thursday's post adds is a presidential endorsement on Truth Social — not a signed contract, not a tariff proclamation, not a CHIPS Act disbursement.

## Market reaction

Intel shares opened Thursday at $125.05, climbed to an intraday high of $128.68 — roughly 3.5% above Wednesday's close of $124.34. A real move, but well below the May 11 all-time high of $132.75, which was driven by the 18A risk-production confirmation rather than any executive post.

For traders trying to price the tariff component specifically, the post offers little purchase. The 25% advanced-chip rate is enacted; the 100% threat is still floating. Without a formal proclamation that maps rates to specific Harmonized Tariff Schedule codes, the supply-chain repricing that would move the broader semiconductor sector stays theoretical.

The actionable catalyst to watch: a Commerce Department Section 232 report on broader chip imports, which trade lawyers and industry groups have been tracking. Until that document lands with concrete rates attached, the gap between White House rhetoric and implementable policy remains open.

warsh-hawkish-fed-debut-october-hike.headline: Warsh kills the easing bias in hawkish Fed debut; October rate hike fully priced in
warsh-hawkish-fed-debut-october-hike.body_md:
Kevin Warsh chaired his first Federal Reserve policy meeting on Wednesday and left little ambiguity about the institution he intends to run. The Federal Open Market Committee held its benchmark rate steady at 3.50%–3.75% — a unanimous 12-to-zero vote, itself a notable contrast to the fractured 8-to-4 split that accompanied the last decision carrying an easing bias — but the surrounding architecture of the decision made plain that the next move is more likely up than down.

Markets did not need much time to work through the implications. Two-year Treasury yields jumped 14 basis points to 4.19%, their highest in more than a year. The S&P 500 fell 1.2% to 7,440, the Russell 2000 lost 2%, and gold dropped 3.4% to around $4,229 an ounce — a rapid reversal of the haven bids that had accumulated on expectations of easier monetary policy. By the close, fed funds futures had fully priced a rate increase by October.

![The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, D.C., where the FOMC convened Wednesday](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0a/Eccles_Building_-_north_side.JPG)

## A Dot Plot That Points the Other Way

The clearest statement came from the Summary of Economic Projections. The median forecast for the federal funds rate at year-end 2026 moved to 3.8% from 3.4% in the March projections — a quarter-point above the current rate rather than below it. Nine of 18 participating officials projected at least one hike this year; six of those expected two or more. Wall Street had entered the session pricing a coin-flip on a cut by mid-year. That trade is now inverted.

Inflation forecasts were revised substantially higher. Personal consumption expenditure inflation for 2026 was lifted to 3.6% from 2.7%. Core PCE moved to 3.3% from 2.7%. These are not rounding errors; they represent a formal acknowledgment that the disinflationary progress assumed in earlier projections has stalled, and that the committee no longer expects it to resume on its own.

Warsh declined to add his own dot. He had long criticized the dot plot as a tool that constrains rather than clarifies policy, and he carried that skepticism directly into the round: "Submitting a dot for myself would not be helpful in the conduct of policy," he said. He offered a colloquial summary of how much conviction attaches to anyone else's submission: "Pencils with big erasers. Policymakers don't feel bound by their dots." The plot survives through year-end under a prior commitment, Warsh confirmed, but a broader communications review — including the SEP's structure, press conference cadence, and the dot format itself — is already underway and expected to conclude by December.

## Scrapping the Roadmap

![Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh](https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/images/chairman-warsh-130x168.png)

Warsh's signature departure from recent practice was the elimination of forward guidance. The decision, he said, "was not well-suited to the current policy conjuncture." Where the Powell-era Fed anchored markets to explicit rate-path language — often at the cost of credibility when conditions shifted — Warsh made clear that decisions would be made meeting by meeting on what the committee sees at the time. "We've dropped forward guidance," he said flatly. "I cannot give any forward guidance about what we will do next."

The commitment he did make was harder-edged. "This committee will deliver price stability," Warsh said at his post-decision press conference. "The commitment to deliver is strong, unanimous, and unambiguous." He was direct about the record the new leadership inherits: "We've missed on inflation for five years and we're going to fix that." He characterized inflation as fundamentally a policy choice — "Inflation is a choice. You bet it is" — framing it as a problem with a solution, not a structural condition to be managed around.

On the degree of restriction already embedded in current policy, Warsh offered a pointed nuance: the Fed's rate level bites mainly in housing and not broadly across financial markets. "It is hard to say policy is restrictive anywhere but in housing," he said — a candid concession that the 3.50%–3.75% range has not yet cooled the wider economy. He also rejected the idea of a forced trade-off: "I don't believe we have a cruel choice between full employment and stable prices." All 19 members at the table felt no need to tighten at Wednesday's meeting, he noted — though the dots reveal many expect tightening soon.

Warsh disclosed that he meets weekly with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, having spoken with him three times since taking office, calling the coordination "very useful." He acknowledged Middle East tensions as a factor that affects the Fed's "day job," even if geopolitical developments fall outside its mandate. The committee is focused, he said, on preventing commodity-specific price increases — oil, eggs, beef — from broadening into the wider economy rather than using them as grounds for a blanket monetary response.

## Four Task Forces and a Year-End Deadline

Alongside the rate decision, Warsh announced four internal task forces designed to modernize how the Fed gathers and interprets the data it acts on. A Balance Sheet task force will review the ample-reserves operating regime. A Data task force will consider new sources and methodologies; Warsh expressed openness to private-sector data and acknowledged that most central bank data still relies on "old-fashioned surveys." A Productivity and Jobs task force will survey the reach of AI and other general-purpose technologies — the committee discussed AI at length on Wednesday, Warsh said, describing it as "filled with opportunity and risks" and noting more certainty about demand-side AI investment than about supply-side capacity. An Inflation Frameworks task force will examine the drivers of inflation; the 2% target itself is explicitly outside scope.

All four begin work in coming weeks, with results expected by fall and final conclusions by year-end. Warsh committed to reporting back, and said he "would not be surprised" if a new communications framework and changes to the SEP follow. He framed it in terms of credibility: "Our credibility requires delivering on promises in all areas."

The internal divisions on rates are real, and Warsh was candid about them. His read on the 19 participants: roughly half felt rates should be lower and half felt they should be higher. That even split, set against a dot plot that now leans toward a hike, suggests the path forward hinges on incoming inflation data rather than on built-in consensus. There was one policy proposal on the table at Wednesday's meeting, he said — discussed briefly, reached after what he called "a good family fight for a couple of days" — and the task forces will make recommendations, not decisions. "We are not outsourcing decisions."

## The October Clock

For fixed-income traders, the session compressed months of rate repricing into a single afternoon. The two-year yield at 4.19% is pricing a world in which the Fed moves at least once more before year-end. The gap between two-year and ten-year yields narrowed to within 30 basis points — the flattest the curve has been in over a year — as the front end bore the brunt of the shift. The dollar index climbed 0.8% past 100, and the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index rose 0.7% against major peers.

"Half the committee is expecting rate hikes this year," said JPMorgan Asset Management's chief investment officer. "That's a real shot across the bow at the market."

Warsh signaled he would not be moved by the reaction: "I won't be particularly intrigued by how markets react in the first minutes, days." That stance, whatever its intent, amounts to a withdrawal of the implicit Fed stabilizer that equity investors have leaned on for years. The so-called Fed put — the market expectation that sufficiently large equity losses would prompt a dovish pivot — is absent from the new playbook. "We've given markets a new chapter for the central bank," Warsh said. "This is a lot of change for financial markets to digest."

Six weeks separate this meeting from the next FOMC gathering. Between now and then, two CPI prints, a payrolls report, and ongoing developments in Middle East energy markets will either validate or complicate the hawkish tilt. The task force results arrive in fall; the potential SEP overhaul in December. Warsh's own communications innovations — new formats, ad hoc press conferences, whatever he described as "some new and interesting things" — remain unspecified but promised. The clearest signal he gave was that the Fed would let the data speak, and would follow financial market prices as its most important source of guidance. How much more change is coming will depend on what both tell him by July.

realreal-vs-rh-luxury-retail.headline: The RealReal vs. RH: two bets on luxury retail in a consumer slowdown
realreal-vs-rh-luxury-retail.body_md:
The luxury goods market has quietly run out of easy fuel. Morgan Stanley forecasts personal luxury goods growth of just 2.5% this year, and Bain & Company notes that roughly 80% of the sector's expansion between 2023 and 2025 came from price increases, not volume. Aspirational buyers are pulling back. The brands built to capture them are reconsidering their playbooks.

The RealReal and RH have arrived at sharply different answers.

The RealReal — the authenticated luxury resale platform now led by co-founder Rati Sahi Levesque — is betting that a slowdown pulls its audience toward it. Membership has crossed 40 million, skewed toward millennials and Gen Z buyers for whom secondhand luxury is a first preference, not a fallback. Some 58% of luxury shoppers now say they favour resale in at least some product categories. First-quarter 2026 gross merchandise volume reached $606 million, up 24% year on year. Total revenue hit $189.7 million, a 19% gain, and the company raised its full-year guidance to $770–$784 million.

![The RealReal consignment store in Greenwich, Connecticut](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c6/The_RealReal_%2853920745977%29.jpg)

The catch is familiar. An accumulated deficit of $1.3 billion and a forward P/E of 187x require the thesis — that scale will eventually convert to cash — to hold longer than investors have often been patient. Adjusted EBITDA guidance for the full year is $59–$67 million: progress, but still a promissory note.

## The lifestyle bet

RH is running a different play: bet that the wealthiest consumers barely notice a slowdown, and spend the downcycle expanding the footprint they'll profit from when conditions ease. First-quarter 2026 revenue came in at $800 million, down 1.7% year on year, partly because tariff-related sourcing disruptions deferred roughly $45 million in sales. A quarterly net loss of $13.7 million followed. Management responded by raising the full-year outlook anyway: 4.5–8% revenue growth, with adjusted free cash flow of $300–$400 million.

The expansion plan is deliberately theatrical. CEO Gary Friedman is opening galleries in London's Mayfair and Milan in 2026, the London site designed by Foster + Partners across three Grade II-listed buildings near Savile Row — with a restaurant, wine bar, and Champagne and caviar bar in the basement. Pre-opening costs are expected to clip roughly 270 basis points from adjusted margins. At a forward P/E of around 30x and a price-to-sales ratio below 1x, investors are not yet pricing in the vision.

The test for each company is specific. For The RealReal, the signal arrives in the next two quarters: whether the raised 2026 guidance converts to meaningful cash generation. For RH, it comes when the London and Milan galleries open — and whether a luxury lifestyle concept conceived in Corte Madera can find its footing on a continent that has never lacked its own.
